The diagram shows axes with a dashed hyperplane boundary line separating a lower region from a half-space H. Parallel above the dashed line is a solid line passing through point x*. A vector arrow q is shown orthogonal to the lines, pointing into a dark cross-hatched half-space containing the point x* + \varepsilon q, representing the set A(x* + \varepsilon q, x*). A shaded strip lies between the solid line and the dashed hyperplane H. At the bottom, a formula states: \int_H g(z) dz > 1/2 \Rightarrow m_{g(\cdot)}(x* + \varepsilon q, x*) > 1/2.

pg_771__page_41_Figure_16.jpeg.description:
The image contains two sub-figures illustrating medians in two-dimensional spaces:

(a) Uniform distribution over a rectangle: A rectangle with a central point labeled x*. A dashed line passing through x* at an angle divides the rectangle into two equal areas, showing that the central point x* is a median as every line passing through it bisects the total area.

(b) Uniform distribution over a triangle: An equilateral triangle with a horizontal dashed line passing through a central point labeled x. The line divides the triangle into a smaller top triangular section and a larger bottom trapezoidal section, demonstrating that no point exists where every line bisects the area into equal halves, and thus there is no median.

pg_771__page_54_Figure_8.jpeg.description:
Two utility possibility sets, denoted as U, plotted on Cartesian axes with u_1 on the horizontal axis and u_2 on the vertical axis.

Left plot: Shows a strictly convex utility possibility frontier bounded by a smooth, downward-sloping curve in the positive quadrant, with the region U shaded underneath it.

Right plot: Shows a linear utility possibility frontier given by a straight line with a negative slope, with the region U shaded underneath it and extending into the surrounding quadrants, representing a transferable utility model.

pg_771__page_57_Figure_13.jpeg.description:
Two graphs illustrating utility possibility sets and Pareto frontiers in economic theory.

On the left, a 2D plot of utility $u_2$ versus utility $u_1$ shows a shaded utility set $U$ bounded by axes and a non-convex curve. Arrows along the boundary indicate parameter limits: $p_2 \to 0$ moving upward along the boundary toward the vertical axis, and $p_2 \to \infty$ moving around a bend in the lower-right region.

On the right, a 3D plot displays utility axes $u_1$, $u_2$, and $u_3$. A shaded surface represents a utility region in three dimensions, with a highlighted curve along the upper edge labeled "Pareto frontier."

pg_771__page_57_Figure_21.jpeg.description: A two-dimensional plot with horizontal axis labeled u1 and vertical axis labeled u2. The shaded region U represents a utility possibility set (UPS). The upper-right boundary of U forms a non-convex step shape: moving from left to right along the boundary, it extends horizontally to the right, drops vertically downward, moves horizontally to the right again, and then drops vertically downward below the u1 axis. This illustrates a non-convex utility possibility set in utility space.

pg_771__page_58_Figure_12.jpeg.description: A 2D coordinate plot depicting a utility possibility set U in utility space with axes u1 (horizontal) and u2 (vertical). The set U is shaded in gray and bounded by a downward-sloping, strictly convex curve (bowed inward toward the origin region) connecting a point on the positive u2-axis to a point on the positive u1-axis. The region extending below and to the left of these boundary lines is shaded, demonstrating a non-convex utility possibility set.

pg_771__page_58_Figure_19.jpeg.description: A microeconomic diagram plotting good $x_{21}$ on the vertical axis against leisure/consumption good $x_{11}$ on the horizontal axis. The horizontal axis ranges up to 1, with a dashed vertical line at $\bar{x}_{11}$, indicating that 'Labor Supply' is the horizontal distance from $\bar{x}_{11}$ to 1. An indifference curve labeled $u_1(\cdot) = u_1$ curves convexly downward, touching a budget-like line tangent at the point $(\bar{x}_{11}, \bar{x}_{21})$. Parallel budget lines slope downwards, intersecting the axes. A vertical bracket indicates the quantity $x_{22}$ as the vertical gap between a higher budget line and the point $(\bar{x}_{11}, \bar{x}_{21})$.

pg_771__page_59_Figure_13.jpeg.description:
Two side-by-side economic graphs illustrating optimal taxation and utility frontiers.

Left Graph: A plot with horizontal axis labeled $x_{11}$ (ranging from 0 to 1) and vertical axis labeled $x_{21}$. A backward-bending 'Offer Curve' intersects a straight budget line with slope $1-t$ at the point $x_1(t)$. The horizontal coordinate of this intersection is marked $x_{11}(t)$. The distance on the $x_{11}$ axis from $x_{11}(t)$ to 1 represents 'Labor Supply'.

Right Graph: Utility space with horizontal axis $u_1$ and vertical axis $u_2$. It displays two utility possibility frontiers: an upper boundary labeled 'First-best Frontier' and an inner boundary labeled 'Second-best Frontier' starting at point $Q$ on the vertical axis, rising to a peak, and then joining the first-best frontier at the horizontal axis.

pg_771__page_61_Figure_12.jpeg.description:
Two graphs illustrating symmetric social welfare functions in utility space with axes $u_1$ (horizontal) and $u_2$ (vertical).

Left graph: Shows two symmetric indifference curves that are invariant when reflected across the $45^\circ$ diagonal line passing through the origin.

Right graph: Shows the interaction between a symmetric, strictly concave utility frontier (curving downwards away from the origin) and a symmetric, convex social indifference curve (curving upwards away from the origin), intersecting tangentially at the $45^\circ$ diagonal line. The feasible utility set $U$ is located beneath the frontier.

pg_771__page_62_Figure_13.jpeg.description:
Three diagrams showing social welfare indifference curves (isowelfare curves) plotted with utility $u_1$ on the horizontal axis and $u_2$ on the vertical axis:

(a) Linear indifference curves: Parallel straight lines sloping downward at a -1 slope, representing a linear (additive) social welfare function where utilities are perfect substitutes.

(b) L-shaped indifference curves: Right-angled curves with vertices along a 45-degree dashed ray from the origin, representing a Rawlsian or Leontief (min-type) social welfare function where utilities are perfect complements.

(c) Convex indifference curves: Smooth, strictly convex curves bowing toward the origin, representing a standard strictly concave utility/social welfare trade-off with diminishing marginal rates of substitution between individual utilities.

pg_771__page_63_Figure_13.jpeg.description: A utility possibility frontier graph plotted on a coordinate plane with horizontal axis u_1 and vertical axis u_2. A shaded feasible utility region U is bounded below by the horizontal axis and above by a concave utility curve labeled Q. A 45-degree dashed ray extends from the origin through the space. The curve u_2 reach its highest point where it intersects the 45-degree ray; this point is labeled 'Maximin Optimum' and lies at the corner of an L-shaped Leontief-type social indifference curve. Further to the right along the utility frontier, a straight line with a slope of -1 is tangent to the curve Q; this point of tangency is labeled 'Utilitarian Optimum'.

pg_771__page_63_Figure_14.jpeg.description: A graph illustrating social welfare optima in utility space, with utility $u_1$ on the horizontal axis and utility $u_2$ on the vertical axis. A thick curve representing the utility possibility frontier is labeled $Q$ on the left and slopes downward to the right, ending at a point on the $u_1$-axis labeled 'First-best Optimum Point'. Along the frontier, several points are highlighted corresponding to different parameters $\rho$ of a social welfare function: a point labeled '$\rho = \infty$' (Rawlsian/maximin criterion) lying near the corner of an L-shaped indifference curve aligned with a $45^\circ$ dashed line from the origin; a point labeled '$\rho = 1$' where a smooth convex indifference curve is tangent to the frontier; and a point labeled '$\rho = 0$' (utilitarian criterion) where a straight downward-sloping linear social indifference line is tangent to the frontier.

pg_771__page_65_Figure_10.jpeg.description:
A two-dimensional utility possibility frontier graph plotted on axes labeled $u_1$ (horizontal axis) and $u_2$ (vertical axis). The graph illustrates two overlapping utility possibility sets (UPS), labeled $U$ and $U'$. 

1. Set $U'$ is represented by a steeper, hatched boundary curve that extends higher along the $u_2$ axis.
2. Set $U$ is represented by a flatter, shaded boundary curve that extends farther out along the $u_1$ axis.
3. The two sets intersect, creating an overlapping region.
4. A specific status-quo utility point $u$ is marked with a black dot on the boundary of set $U$ (inside the region also covered by $U'$).
5. An alternative utility point $\hat{u}$ is marked with a black dot on the boundary of set $U$ farther to the right, outside set $U'$.
6. The figure demonstrates the weak compensation test where $U'$ allows reaching utility combinations superior to $u$ for some allocations.

pg_771__page_66_Figure_11.jpeg.description: A graph plotting two utility possibility sets, U and U', on axes u1 (horizontal) and u2 (vertical). The boundary curve of utility set U is flatter and extends further right along the u1 axis, while the boundary curve of U' is steeper and extends higher along the u2 axis. The two frontier curves intersect in the positive quadrant. Set U' is shaded with diagonal hatching, while set U is shaded with gray stippling, creating an overlapping region. Point u lies on the frontier of U inside set U', and point u' lies on the frontier of U' inside set U, illustrating a paradox in the weak compensation test.

pg_771__page_70_Figure_14.jpeg.description: A graph on a Cartesian coordinate system with horizontal axis u_1 and vertical axis u_2, illustrating the indifference map of a social welfare function. Three parallel convex indifference curves are plotted in the utility space. A dashed line passing through the origin at a 45-degree angle represents the vector e = (1,1). Arrows connecting corresponding points across the three curves indicate that each curve is a parallel translation of the others along the direction of vector e (the 45-degree line), illustrating invariance to identical changes of utility origins.

pg_771__page_71_Figure_12.jpeg.description: A geometric diagram plotting utility levels $u_1$ on the horizontal axis and $u_2$ on the vertical axis, illustrating the construction of a social welfare function invariant to identical changes of origin. A 45-degree ray extends from the origin through points $W(u)e$, $\bar{u}e$, $W(u')e$, $\bar{u}'e$, and $e$. Two convex social indifference curves, representing utility vectors $u$ and $u' = u + (\bar{u}' - \bar{u})e$, are shown alongside parallel straight lines with slope -1 that pass through these utility vectors and intersect the 45-degree line. The diagram highlights two segments of equal length along the 45-degree ray: one between $W(u)e$ and $\bar{u}e$, and another between $W(u')e$ and $\bar{u}'e$, demonstrating how utility vectors are translated parallel to the line of equality ($e$) to construct invariant social rankings.

pg_771__page_75_Figure_18.jpeg.description: A graph depicting the symmetry property for bargaining solutions in a two-player utility space ($u_1, u_2$). The horizontal axis represents utility $u_1$ and the vertical axis represents utility $u_2$. A shaded region labeled $U$ represents a 'Symmetric Set' of feasible utility allocations, bounded by a curved outer boundary that is symmetric with respect to the $45^\circ$ line passing through the origin. The origin is marked as the 'Threat Point'. A dashed line at a $45^\circ$ angle extends from the origin through the intersection with the upper boundary of $U$, where a point is labeled $f(U)$, representing the symmetric bargaining solution outcome.

pg_771__page_76_Figure_12.jpeg.description: A two-dimensional plot with horizontal axis labeled u (or u1) and vertical axis labeled u2. The origin at (0,0) is marked with a black dot labeled "Threat Point". Two nested utility regions are shown: a smaller region U' shaded lightly, and a larger region U containing U' (with the non-overlapping parts stippled). A single boundary point where the boundaries of U and U' touch is highlighted with a black dot and labeled f(U) = f(U'), illustrating the property of independence of irrelevant alternatives for bargaining solutions.

pg_771__page_77_Figure_14.jpeg.description: A 2D graph depicting an egalitarian bargaining solution in utility space. The vertical axis is labeled 'u_2' and the horizontal axis is labeled 'u_1'. The origin (0,0) is marked as a black dot labeled 'Threat Point'. A shaded region labeled 'U' represents the feasible utility set, bounded by the axes and a downward-sloping concave curve on the upper right. A dashed line emanates from the origin at a 45-degree angle (labeled '45°'). The intersection point of this 45-degree line and the boundary of the feasible set U is marked with a black dot and labeled 'f_e(U)', representing the egalitarian solution point.

pg_771__page_77_Figure_15.jpeg.description:
A graph illustrating the utilitarian bargaining solution on a utility possibility set U plotted on axes u1 (horizontal) and u2 (vertical).

- The shaded region represents the utility set U, bounded above by a concave curve in the upper-right quadrant.
- The origin (0,0) is marked with a point labeled 'Threat Point'.
- A line tangent to the upper boundary of U has a perpendicular normal vector pointing in the direction (1, 1), indicated by an arrow and a right-angle symbol.
- The point of tangency between this line and the boundary of U is marked with a black dot, labeled as f_u(U), which is the utilitarian solution.
- A parallel line lies further out, showing equal-payoff lines (u1 + u2 = constant) maximized at the tangency point.

pg_771__page_77_Figure_17.jpeg.description: A graph illustrating the Nash solution for bargaining problems (Figure 22.E.5). The vertical axis is labeled u_2 and the horizontal axis represents u_1. The origin (0,0) is identified as the 'Threat Point'. A region labeled U represents the feasible utility payoffs. The point f_n(U) lies on the upper frontier of region U, where a hyperbola given by u_1 * u_2 = constant is tangent to the boundary of U. A straight line tangent to U at f_n(U) intersects the vertical axis at point b and the horizontal axis at point a. At the top of the diagram, an equation states: Length [b, f_n(U)] = Length [f_n(U), a], demonstrating that the Nash solution bisects the segment of the tangent line between the coordinate axes.

pg_771__page_78_Figure_13.jpeg.description:
A geometric diagram in the utility space (u1, u2) illustrating the Nash bargaining solution and its relationship to utilitarian and egalitarian solutions under rescaling. The horizontal axis represents u1 and the vertical axis u2. A shaded feasible utility region U lies in the positive quadrant, bounded by a curved Pareto frontier. The origin is labeled as the "Threat Point".

At the frontier point (û1, û2), a hyperbolic level curve represented by "ln u1 + ln u2 = constant" is tangent to the boundary of U. The normal vector to this tangent line at (û1, û2) is given by (1/û1, 1/û2) = ∇(ln u1 + ln u2). A straight line passing through the origin and (û1, û2) forms an angle/slope indicated by η1/η2. Along this line, the optimal point satisfies (û1, û2) = (γ/η1, γ/η2).

Another perpendicular vector labeled (η1, η2) points outward from a linear boundary tangent to the curve, illustrating how rescaling utility weights (η1, η2) aligns the gradient direction with the line of equal utility ratios from the threat point.

pg_771__page_79_Figure_11.jpeg.description:
Two graphs illustrating bargaining solutions in two-player utility space (u1, u2).

Left graph (Figure 22.E.7): Illustrates the Nash bargaining solution. The axes u1 and u2 originate from the 'Threat Point' at (0,0). Three utility sets are shown: U, U', and U''. The line passing through (0,2) and (2,0) represents a symmetric set U'' where the point (1,1) = f(U'') is the outcome. By Independence of Irrelevant Alternatives and invariance properties, the point hat{u} = f_n(U) = f(U') = f(U) is uniquely determined on the Pareto frontier of U at the tangency point with the hyperbola.

Right graph (Figure 22.E.8): Illustrates the Kalai-Smorodinsky solution f_k(U). The Threat Point is at the origin (0,0). The maximum achievable individual utilities are u^2(U) on the vertical axis u2 and u^1(U) on the horizontal axis u1. A straight line connects the Threat Point (0,0) to the ideal point (u^1(U), u^2(U)). The Kalai-Smorodinsky solution f_k(U) is located at the intersection of this line connecting the origin to the ideal point and the Pareto boundary of set U, labeled as 'Midpoint'.

pg_771__page_80_Figure_9.jpeg.description:
A two-dimensional utility space plot depicting bargaining solutions and the lack of monotonicity for different social choice rules. The horizontal axis represents agent 1's utility ($u_1$) and the vertical axis represents agent 2's utility ($u_2$).

The origin $(0,0)$ is labeled as the 'Threat Point'. A dashed line extends from the origin at a $45^\circ$ angle.
Two utility feasible sets are shown: set $U$ and a shaded extended set $U'$.
- For set $U$, a vertex on the upper frontier represents $f_u(U) = f_n(U) = f_k(U)$, indicating that the Utilitarian, Nash, and Kalai-Smorodinsky solutions coincide at this point, while the egalitarian solution $f_e(U)$ lies below it on the same vertical line.
- For the expanded set $U'$, the point on the $45^\circ$ line along the outer Pareto frontier represents the point where all four bargaining solutions coincide: $f_u(U') = f_n(U') = f_k(U') = f_e(U')$.
Key points on the axes are marked at $4$ on both the $u_1$ and $u_2$ axes.
